This document collects supporting analyses for the main text. Section references,
metric names (PC1, PC2, ΔMMR) and methods follow the main paper.

# Per-server data summary {#sec-data}

The corpus is 92.7 million ranked games from the top ~1,000 players on each of
eight regional servers. Servers differ by an order of magnitude in game volume,
from 2.3 million games on OC1 to 30.1 million on EUW1 (@tbl-servers). They also
differ sharply in how many players carry an individually significant circadian
phase: **JP1 is an extreme outlier**, with roughly three quarters of its players
reaching the Benjamini–Hochberg threshold on both behavioural components, against
10–28% everywhere else. This is a symptom of JP1's daily maintenance shutdown
(~05:00–11:00 local; main-text Figure 1): the truncated sampling window makes the
fitted 24 h sinusoid look artificially strong and places its peak in unsampled
hours. We therefore **exclude JP1 from all phase-based analyses** (the FDR
fractions, the modality fits and the kernel density); it is retained only in the
period analysis and the play-volume figure. The per-server row for JP1 below is
shown for completeness and is flagged accordingly.

| Server | Ranked games | PC1 significant | PC2 significant |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| BR1  | 10.35 M | 9.6% | 5.9% |
| EUN1 | 13.55 M | 11.0% | 6.8% |
| EUW1 | 30.15 M | 17.6% | 20.5% |
| LA1  | 3.81 M | 9.1% | 3.1% |
| LA2  | 2.91 M | 9.6% | 1.5% |
| NA1  | 17.15 M | 25.4% | 28.4% |
| OC1  | 2.33 M | 16.9% | 5.7% |

# Within-subject rhythm summary {#sec-within}

Each server's within-subject periodogram peaks within a few minutes of 24.0 h for
both behavioural components and for ΔMMR (@fig-within, left; JP1's two flagged
harmonic peaks are the outliers screened from the period meta-analysis): the
circadian period is not a pooled artefact but recurs server by server, with the
N-weighted mean sitting on 24 h. The fraction of players carrying an individually
significant phase separates behaviour from success (@fig-within, right; JP1
excluded): 14.2% of players for PC1 and 10.3% for PC2, against 0.3% for ΔMMR.
Skill *change* has almost no per-player circadian signal, which is why it cannot
be tested for modality.

![Within-subject rhythm summary. **Left:** best period from each server's player-level periodogram for PC1, PC2 and ΔMMR; all sit on 24 h (dashed), with the N-weighted mean ± SEM overlaid. **Right:** weighted fraction of analysed players whose peak phase was FDR-significant, by metric.](../results/GRAND/grand_within_subject_summary.png){#fig-within width=100%}

# Phase variation is not inherited from the play-time schedule {#sec-playtime}

The wide individual spread of behavioural peak phases (main text) is not an echo
of *when* people play. A natural worry is that the behavioural phases only
reproduce the shape of the play-time schedule. We tested this directly. For each
analysed player we took the circular-mean hour of their games in local time —
their preferred play time — and pooled these across servers (7,966 players), then
described the distribution with the same circular fits used for the behavioural
phases. This complements Figure 1 of the main text, which makes the point at the
level of the *server*: aggregate play volume follows a single evening-peaked
curve on every server once local time is used. Here we ask about individual
*players*.

The preferred-play-time distribution is single-peaked and comparatively *tight*
(@fig-playtime, @tbl-playtime): it concentrates in the evening around 19.6 h with
a concentration of $\kappa \approx 2.6$ (circular standard deviation ≈ 3 h), and
BIC prefers one component over two (ΔBIC = 1.8 in favour of the single component).
The behavioural peak phases, by contrast, are single-moded but spread more than
twice as widely (circular standard deviation ≈ 7 h; main text @sec-bimodality).
Players cluster their log-on times into the evening far more tightly than their
behaviour peaks, so the broad individual variation in behavioural phase is a
property of how players behave at a given hour, not of the hours they choose to
play.

![Per-player preferred play time, pooled across servers (N = 7,966). **Left:** distribution of each player's circular-mean play hour (local), with one-component (dashed) and two-component (solid, dotted components) von Mises fits. **Right:** the same fits in polar view. The distribution has a single evening peak near 19.6 h; BIC prefers one component.](../results/GRAND/grand_play_time_chronotype.png){#fig-playtime width=100%}

| Metric | N players | log L (1) | log L (2) | ΔAIC (1−2) | ΔBIC (1−2) | Preferred | Bootstrap $p$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|:--|:--|
| Play time | 7,966 | −8,736.8 | −8,724.2 | 19.2 | −1.8 | 1-component | <.001 |

: One- versus two-component circular fit to pooled preferred play times.
  A negative ΔBIC favours the single component: play time is single-peaked, as
  are the behavioural peak phases in the main text (@sec-bimodality), but the
  play-time distribution is far more concentrated (κ ≈ 2.6 vs ≈ 0.4).
  {#tbl-playtime}
